e.t: Abirōn, also rendered Aviron, is a proper name referring to a particular person rather than a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX entity, it occurs 11 times. Most occurrences are in Numbers, with additional occurrences in Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Kings, and 4 Maccabees. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is primarily identifying: it distinguishes the individual called Abirōn or Aviron. The exact significance of each mention depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective means “Egyptian,” identifying a person or thing connected with Egypt. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Genesis, and serves to mark Egyptian identity. The word appears in Genesis 16:1, Genesis 16:3, and Genesis 21:9. Its basic sense is geographical or national: it describes someone or something associated with Egypt rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. The surrounding verse determines exactly what Egyptian person or thing is being identified.

This Greek LXX adjective means “uncovered” or “unveiled.” It describes something that is not covered or hidden, emphasizing its exposed or plainly visible state. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Epistle of Jeremiah 1:30. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense remains the absence of a covering or concealment.

This verb means to follow—to go after someone or continue along with them. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes the basic act of following a person or course rather than naming a particular emotion or doctrine. It occurs eight times in this LXX corpus: seven times in the Old Testament books and once in the deuterocanonical writings. Its precise force in any passage depends on who is being followed and the surrounding sentence.

This noun refers to a headland or foreland—a piece of land that projects outward, especially toward a body of water or surrounding area. It is a geographical term describing a prominent extension of land rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs 22 times, showing that it is used as a normal place-word across several books. Its exact sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the location being described.

This Greek LXX adverb describes an action done “strangely” or “hostilely.” It can indicate conduct that is unusual or marked by opposition toward someone. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Isaiah 28:21, so its normal meaning is clear, but its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage. It functions by describing how an action is carried out, rather than naming a person, object, or event.

Ambri, also rendered Amvri, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe a general quality or action; it identifies an individual by name. The name occurs 16 times in 14 verses, from 1 Kings 16:16 through 2 Chronicles 22:2. Most of its occurrences are in 1 Kings, with additional occurrences in 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, and 2 Chronicles. Scripture preserves the name as a personal designation rather than giving it a separate descriptive meaning.

Ammaous is a proper name, referring to a named person, place, or other particular entity rather than describing an action or quality. It is also given as “Ammaus,” an alternate rendering of the same name. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs four times, all in 1 Maccabees. Its exact reference depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic function remains that of identifying a specific name, not expressing a general concept.

gl: sth to recline on; back of a chair
d: sth to recline on; back of a chair

e.t: This noun refers to something a person reclines on, especially the back of a chair. It names a physical support used when sitting or resting, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Song of Songs 3:10. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a place or part of furniture that supports someone who reclines.

This adjective describes a person who murders a husband—that is, a husband murderer. It identifies the person by the act of killing a man who is someone’s husband. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:28. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains clear: one who murders a husband.

This word means “register”. It is a verb describing the act of entering or listing people or information in an official record. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including once in Proverbs and four times in 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on formally recording something, while the surrounding passage determines what is being registered and why. [p03:word:lxx:L701437:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L701437:occurrences]

This LXX verb means “angry,” describing the state of being angry. It functions as an action or state word: it tells the reader that someone is experiencing anger, rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical sense is clear: it expresses anger.

Asma, also rendered Azma, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a named person or title within the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs 15 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing from Numbers through Song of Songs. Its precise referent depends on the passage where it occurs, but the lexical evidence supports treating it as a name, not expanding it into an additional descriptive meaning.

Desert means to leave or abandon a person, group, or cause, especially by withdrawing one’s support or allegiance. It is a verb describing the act of departing from those one was expected to remain with. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, from Joshua through 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is desertion.

Achiman, also rendered Akhiman, is a proper name used to identify a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Numbers 13:22. The name itself functions as a personal designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific role in that passage cannot be explained further, but its basic meaning is the person’s name, Achiman.

Baalath is a proper name, also rendered “Vaalath.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Kings 2:35 and 2 Chronicles 8:6. The supplied lexical information gives the name’s forms but does not provide enough context to explain more about the person, place, or thing identified by it.

This word is a proper name: “Basēdōth; Vasithoth.” It identifies a named person, place, or other entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:39. The available name itself does not establish whether it refers to a person or location, so its precise role depends on the surrounding verse. Its main meaning is therefore its identity as the name Basēdōth, also rendered Vasithoth, rather than a general word with a broader definition.

Beni, also rendered Veni, is a proper name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a person by name. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Nehemiah 3:18. Since the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the name itself can be explained, but no further detail about the person or the context should be added.

Gamer is a proper name, referring to a person named Gamer rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, rendered consistently as “Gamer.” The name occurs in Genesis 10:2–3 and 1 Chronicles 1:5–6. Its meaning here is therefore its identifying use as a personal name; the surrounding verse context would be needed to explain the person’s particular role in any one passage.

This word is a proper name rendered “Gedsōni” or “Yethsoni.” It identifies a named individual or group designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: in Numbers 26:57 and 2 Chronicles 29:12. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name’s specific reference in each passage cannot be described more precisely.

This verb means “taste sweet”: it describes something having a sweet taste when it is tasted. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 3:3. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s basic meaning can be stated confidently, while its precise force in that sentence belongs to the wider context. It is a sensory word about sweetness experienced by tasting.

This Greek LXX verb means “lend” or “borrow”: it describes giving something to another person temporarily or receiving it from someone else. The direction depends on the sentence—one person lends, while another borrows. It is used 23 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, with especially frequent use in Deuteronomy. Its references include lending and borrowing in Deuteronomy, Nehemiah, and Psalms, showing its ordinary use for an exchange involving a debt or obligation.

This Greek LXX noun means “afternoon,” referring to the part of the day after midday and before evening. It names a time of day rather than an action, person, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 22:18. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary meaning is simply the afternoon or later daytime period.

This word means “come on,” an expression that urges people to move, join in, or take action. It functions as an adverb or interjection, so it commonly serves as a direct call rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 40 times, showing repeated use for an immediate appeal or summons. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and situation.

This verb means “run off” or “get away.” It describes leaving quickly or escaping from a place or situation rather than remaining present. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it appears twice, once in Sirach and once in 2 Maccabees. These occurrences show that the word names an act of departure or escape; the precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context.

This noun means a “traverse” or “beam”—a structural piece extending across or through something. It names a physical object rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 35:11. The precise reference to a traverse or beam is part of the tabernacle’s construction vocabulary, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular role there.

This adjective means “glorified” or “glorious.” It describes someone or something regarded as possessing honor, splendor, or elevated distinction. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 26:19, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The related English rendering is “glorious,” which agrees with the central sense of the word. It is best understood as a describing word for a person or thing marked by glory or honor.

This noun refers to an “inward part”—something located within rather than on the outside. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 50:12, so its normal sense is narrowly attested in this corpus. The word points to something internal, while the precise force of its use in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The verse text is not included here, so its broader contextual significance cannot be stated from this word alone.

This adjective refers to something connected with sacrifice made to an idol—an offering associated with idol worship. It describes the sacrificed thing or the act of sacrificing it, rather than naming a person. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 5:2. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse text, but its central meaning is clearly tied to an idol’s sacrifice.

This verb means to hinder someone or something, or to prevent it from proceeding. It describes an action that blocks, restrains, or keeps something from taking place. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:18. The word’s basic sense is therefore active and practical: it expresses stopping or obstructing rather than merely delaying or disagreeing. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or action being hindered.

This adjective means “very bright,” describing something that shines with exceptional brilliance or stands out for its intense brightness. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, in Wisdom 17:5. Its meaning points to unusually strong or radiant brightness rather than ordinary light. Since the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the word’s precise force in that passage depends on its context.

This Greek LXX noun means “vomiting,” referring to the act of bringing food or other contents up from the stomach. It names a physical bodily event rather than a person, action of speech, or moral quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Proverbs 33:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the bodily act of vomiting.

This Greek LXX noun means “signal”: a communicated indication meant to draw attention or convey something. It names the signal itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 6:13. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its precise force in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic lexical sense remains a signal, and it belongs to the Greek LXX wording rather than to a separate New Testament Greek entity.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “use charms; sing to.” It describes an action involving spoken or sung words, apparently as a performed utterance rather than a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Jeremiah 8:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to charming or singing words directed toward an intended effect.

It means “longed for,” referring to something desired or yearned after. As a noun, it names the object of longing rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Jeremiah 20:14. That single occurrence shows its rarity within this corpus, while its stated sense gives the basic meaning. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek verb means “hasten”: to move quickly or cause something to happen sooner. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament (including its deuterocanonical books), it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:7. That single occurrence establishes its basic sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly who or what is hastened there. The word’s central idea is urgency or speed, whether referring to movement, action, or the bringing about of an event.

This word is a proper name rendered “Esdran” or “Ezthran.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 8:13. Because the available information gives the name and reference but not the verse text or surrounding passage, the name itself does not establish further details about the person. Its ordinary meaning is therefore the personal name Esdran, also represented as Ezthran.

This adjective means “of good courage,” describing someone who is courageous, confident, or heartened rather than fearful. It expresses a condition of inner strength and readiness to act with courage. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees 8:21 and 3 Maccabees 1:7. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine how that quality is expressed in either passage.

Euma is a proper name preserved as “Euma” in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. The available record contains one occurrence, in Joshua 15:54, so its precise referent—whether a person or a place—must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, not from the name alone. The English rendering simply carries the name over without translating it into a descriptive word.

This noun refers to a venomous snake—an “adder” or “viper.” It identifies a real kind of dangerous serpent rather than an abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish books, it occurs 18 times, showing that the word is used across several scriptural settings for this creature. The precise force of the image in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context.

Zathouia is a proper name, also represented as Zathoia. It identifies a named individual or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Nehemiah 10:15. The available information establishes the name and its occurrence, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the person or group identified there.

This noun means “taking alive”—capturing a person without killing them. It describes the act or result of seizing someone alive rather than destroying them. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:35. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here; its basic meaning remains the capture of a living person.

Thaphthōth, also rendered Thafthoth, is a proper name referring to a particular place or locality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 17:7. The name itself identifies the place; the available wording does not provide an additional definition or describe its features, people, or significance. Its precise geographic role must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This Greek LXX noun means a “bag” or “pouch”—a container used to carry something. It refers to an ordinary physical object, not an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 5:23, and the surrounding verse context determines exactly how the container functions there. The word’s basic sense remains a small receptacle for holding or transporting items.

Thōlai, also rendered Thole, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Numbers 26:19. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide a further ordinary-language definition or explain the person or designation it identifies. Its precise significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and context.

Iallelēl, also rendered Iallelil, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or designation in the Greek Old Testament tradition, so its meaning is primarily the name itself rather than a translated concept. This form occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 29:12. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

Igaal is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, in Numbers 13:7 and 2 Samuel 23:36. Because it is a proper name, its meaning here is primarily the identification of a person; the name itself does not describe the person’s character or role. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Idoua is a proper name, rendered as “Idoua; Ithua.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 12:22. The available lexical information establishes the name’s identity, but the reference alone does not provide enough verse text to explain which person it identifies or what role that person has in the passage. Its precise significance there therefore depends on the surrounding text.

This Greek LXX noun means “clothing”—the garments or apparel a person wears. It refers broadly to what someone puts on, whether ordinary dress or more valuable garments. The word occurs 30 times in the LXX corpus, showing a normal term for clothing across its uses rather than a word limited to one special kind of dress. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the clothes or garments themselves.

This LXX noun means “anything set upright”—something placed or standing in an upright position. It names an upright object or structure rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense appears across several passages without being limited to one setting. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains something established vertically or made to stand upright.

This Greek LXX word means “and” or “even.” It commonly joins words, phrases, or thoughts, and it can also add emphasis or include an additional point. As a conjunction, it links ideas; in other uses, it highlights something with the sense of “even.” It is extremely common in the Greek Old Testament, occurring 54,421 times, so its precise force depends on how it connects the surrounding words in each passage.

This verb means to fill up with something—to make something full or thoroughly supplied. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:46, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic idea remains straightforward: something becomes filled with whatever is being supplied or placed within it.

gl: melt away; make to fall away
d: melt away; make to fall away

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “melt away” or “make to fall away.” It describes something being caused to lose its firmness, substance, or standing, whether by dissolving or being brought down. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or thing. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Micah 4:13; the precise force in that verse is determined by its surrounding passage.

This verb means to “prick” or “goad”—to pierce or prod with a sharp point. It describes an action rather than a person or object, expressing the act of causing a sharp touch or urging movement through such a prod. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 6:4. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense remains the act of pricking or goading.

This adjective means “for putting in motion,” describing something that causes movement or sets something in motion. It points to an active function rather than merely describing motion itself. In the Greek of Wisdom, it occurs once, at Wisdom 7:24, so its precise force there belongs to that passage’s surrounding description. The word’s central idea remains the capacity or role of initiating movement. This is a Greek LXX word, distinct from related Greek New Testament vocabulary.

This Greek LXX noun refers to the inner parts of the body, especially the womb. It can describe bodily insides in a general sense or the womb as the place associated with carrying a child. The word occurs 98 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its exact sense depends on the sentence where it appears. Its central idea remains the body’s inward region rather than an outward limb or surface.

This Greek LXX noun means “attendance; care”—the attention or practical concern given to someone or something. It points to being present to help, look after, or tend to a need, rather than merely noticing it. The word occurs once in the Greek text represented here, in 4 Maccabees 3:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is attentive care expressed through attendance.

This word means “hod,” a noun naming the object referred to by that term. Its exact use must be understood from the surrounding verse, since no verse text is available here. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Judges: Judges 5:25 and Judges 6:38. Thus, its established lexical meaning is clear, while the particular role or significance of the hod in either passage depends on the immediate context.

This Greek LXX verb means “bathe”: it describes the act of bathing or washing oneself. It is an action word, not the name of a person, object, or result. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 44 times in 44 verses, making it a recurring word. Its uses extend from Exodus through Song of Songs, with especially frequent occurrence in Leviticus. The precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the act of bathing.

Mageddō is a proper name for a place known in the Greek Old Testament as Mageddo, also rendered Mayeththo. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Joshua, 2 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any one passage comes from that passage’s surrounding text.

This word is a proper name rendered “Maked” or “Maketh.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees: 5:26 and 5:36. Since the surrounding verse text is not included, the name’s particular reference in each passage cannot be explained further here. Its basic meaning is therefore the preserved name itself: Maked, also rendered Maketh.

This Greek LXX verb means “fight”: to engage in conflict or struggle against someone. It describes active opposition rather than a merely private disagreement. The word appears 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of conflict. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains contending against another person or opposing side.

e.h: A Greek Word for No More
e.t: This Greek LXX adverb means “no more.” It marks that something is to stop, cease, or not happen again. The word can describe the end of a previous action, condition, or supply, so its precise force depends on what it modifies in the sentence. It occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing a repeated use for expressing cessation or discontinuation. Its meaning remains focused: what was happening before is no longer to continue.

This Greek LXX noun means “wages”: payment given in return for work or service. It refers to what a person receives as compensation, especially in a working arrangement. The word appears 56 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, showing a recurring reference to earned payment. Its basic meaning remains focused on the compensation itself rather than on the particular kind of work or the person who pays it.

Nageb, also rendered Nayev, is a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It identifies a named place or region in the Greek Old Testament, appearing ten times across ten verses. Its use is concentrated in Joshua, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Obadiah, showing that it functions as a geographical designation in several Old Testament settings. The name itself does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual principle; the surrounding verse is needed to identify the particular location being mentioned.

Nooza is a proper name, used to identify a particular named person or entity rather than describe an action, quality, or idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 11:30, and is rendered as “Nooza.” The name itself does not provide a wider definition or meaning in ordinary English; its role is identification. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain whom it identifies there.

This noun describes a “mad passion” or an “impulse”—a powerful, sudden drive that can seize a person. It points to intense inner force rather than a calm, deliberate decision. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 2:4. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact force in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context. Its basic sense, however, is a passionate or impulsive movement within a person.

This noun means a portent: a sign regarded as pointing to or foreshadowing something significant. It refers to an omen or remarkable sign rather than an ordinary event. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including passages in Genesis and Numbers. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a portent or sign with special significance.

This Greek LXX noun means “winter fig,” referring to a fig associated with the winter season. It names a particular kind of fruit rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, in Song of Songs 2:13. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning remains a winter fig.

Oudan, also rendered Uthan, is a proper name referring to a person. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, this name occurs once, at 2 Samuel 24:6. The name itself identifies someone, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that person’s specific role or significance there.

e.h: Draw a Crowd or Stir Up
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to “draw a crowd” or “stir up.” It describes causing people to gather or provoking a public disturbance, depending on the surrounding sentence. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Amos 7:16, so its precise force there must be understood from the verse and its context. Its basic idea concerns influencing or agitating a group of people rather than acting privately.

This adjective describes someone or something that surveys or observes everything. It presents a comprehensive view, with nothing outside the range of notice. In the Greek text of Wisdom, the word occurs once, in Wisdom 7:23. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise role in that sentence depends on the context, but its central meaning is “all-surveying.”

This verb means to read publicly—to voice written words so that other people can hear them. It describes an outward, shared act of reading rather than merely looking over a text privately. In its Greek LXX usage, it appears twice, both times in the deuterocanonical books: once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. The basic idea remains straightforward: a person reads aloud before an audience or gathered people. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This Greek LXX verb means “pass” or “transgress.” It can describe moving past or crossing over, and it can also describe going beyond an accepted boundary or command. The word appears 138 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its precise force depends on whether the surrounding passage concerns movement or wrongdoing. Its broad use includes both ordinary passing and the serious idea of transgression.

This noun means “try” or “trial”—an attempt, testing, or ordeal that examines a person or situation. It refers to the experience or process of being tested rather than to a person who tests others. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Deuteronomy and twice in Wisdom. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on an attempt or on a difficult testing experience.

This Greek LXX noun means “fatness,” referring to bodily or material richness and abundance. It appears eleven times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages rendered with the same English term in Genesis, Judges, and 1 Kings. The word can describe physical fatness, but its broader sense may also concern richness or plenty, depending on the surrounding verse. Because the verse texts are not included here, its precise force in any one passage must be understood from that passage’s context.

This Greek LXX verb means “increase”: to become greater in amount, extent, or number. It describes growth or multiplication rather than a fixed object or quality. The word appears 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, with occurrences beginning in Exodus and continuing through 2 Maccabees. As a verb, it expresses the action or process of becoming more. The precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

This noun means “wealth; richness”: an abundance of possessions or resources. It names material prosperity rather than an action, person, or quality of character. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears 95 times, so it is a regularly used word for riches across these writings. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains substantial material abundance.

This word means “gentle.” It describes a person or quality characterized by gentleness rather than harshness. It can function as an adjective describing someone or something, and it can also be used as a noun for one identified by this quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 16 times, including passages in Numbers, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “offer” or “bring to”: it describes moving something or someone toward a recipient, especially as an act of presentation. It appears 148 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, with frequent use in Leviticus and Numbers. Thus, the word can describe the practical act of bringing something forward, while the surrounding sentence identifies what is brought and to whom.

This Greek LXX noun means “fall.” It refers to the act or event of falling, and may describe a fall in a literal or figurative sense depending on the surrounding passage. The word occurs 36 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing that it is used across several kinds of writing rather than being limited to one setting. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the context in which the fall is mentioned.

Rekom, also rendered Rhekom, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore its identification of a named person, place, or other specific subject in the text, though the available lexical information does not specify which.
